The Guianan puffbird (Notharchus macrorhynchos) exhibits several distinctive life-history traits that align with its position as a medium-sized member of the Bucconidae. This relatively modest metabolic expenditure is consistent with the species' sit-and-wait foraging strategy, which minimizes energetic costs between prey captures. The species also demonstrates a constrained reproductive capacity; females typically produce a single clutch of 1 to 2 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per nest], and field observations suggest that they may initiate one to two nesting attempts per year [F_R_i = one to two nesting attempts per year]. This low fecundity is characteristic of many tropical bird species that invest heavily in prolonged parental care rather than maximizing offspring number.

Neonatal body mass in the Guianan puffbird has been recorded at approximately 11 grams [Wwb = approximately 11 grams], a value that reflects the altricial condition typical of this family. Newly hatched chicks are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning and are brooded continuously during their first week. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity, occurring well within the first year of life, contrasts with the species' delayed entry into breeding. Once sexually mature, individuals do not immediately engage in reproduction; instead, a significant period of deferred breeding is observed. The first successful brood is typically initiated at 1.5 years after hatching [tR = 1.5 years after hatching], a delay likely associated with the need to establish a territory, acquire a mate, and accumulate sufficient foraging experience within the complex forest understory that this species inhabits at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].

The ultimate body mass attained by adult Guianan puffbirds differs between the sexes, a common pattern among bucconids. This modest sexual size dimorphism, with females being on average about four percent heavier than males, is thought to relate to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. This longevity is notable for a bird of this mass and suggests that adult survivorship is high, likely owing to the species' concealed nesting habits and its largely predator-avoidance-based lifestyle in the Neotropical lowland forests.

Comparative analyses within the Bucconidae reveal that the Guianan puffbird occupies an intermediate position along several life-history axes. Its adult body mass of 125 grams [Wwi = 125 grams] places it among the larger puffbirds, yet its fledging period of 20.5 days after hatching [tx = 20.5 days after hatching] is compressed relative to what might be predicted allometrically, a trait that may reduce cumulative nest predation risk at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The observed longevity of approximately 3,869 days [am = approximately 3,869 days] for individuals active at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] aligns well with expectations for tropical insectivorous birds, which often exhibit extended lifespans compared to their temperate counterparts.
